case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Hawaii’s restrictions on carrying firearms in public (and the lower courts’ reliance on expert-driven historical/legal interpretations and public-safety balancing) violate the Second Amendment under the history-and-tradition framework required by Bruen.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. amend. II (as incorporated against the States through the Fourteenth Amendment); Federal Rule of Evidence 702 (as to the admissibility/scope of expert testimony in Second Amendment historical-analogy litigation).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners argue that the Second Amendment protects ordinary, law-abiding citizens’ right to carry firearms for self-defense and that Hawaii’s challenged carry restrictions cannot survive Bruen because the State cannot identify sufficiently analogous founding-era (or otherwise relevant historical) firearm regulations to justify them. They further contend that lower courts err when they (1) dilute or disregard Heller/McDonald/Bruen’s holdings, (2) allow public-safety or empirical policy balancing to override the ‘core’ of a right singled out for constitutional protection, and (3) admit or rely on expert testimony that effectively tells the court what the law is—i.e., offers legal conclusions about how to interpret founding-era statutes and whether Supreme Court holdings were ‘historically accurate’—which they argue falls outside Rule 702 and invades the court’s duty to decide questions of law.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondent (Hawaii) maintains that its firearm-carry regulations are constitutional under Bruen because they are consistent with the Nation’s historical tradition of firearm regulation, including historical limits on armed carriage in sensitive places and other longstanding public-carry controls. Hawaii also suggests that historical evidence can be marshaled—often through historians or other experts—to explain the meaning, context, and operation of historical laws, supporting the State’s claim that modern regulations have adequate historical analogues. To the extent public-safety considerations appear in the briefing, the State’s position is that regulation can coexist with the right and that Second Amendment doctrine leaves room for governments to address local social problems so long as the regulations fit within historically recognized limits.
key_precedents: District of Columbia v. Heller, 554 U.S. 570 (2008)
McDonald v. City of Chicago, 561 U.S. 742 (2010)
New York State Rifle & Pistol Ass’n v. Bruen, 597 U.S. 1 (2022)
Commodores Entertainment Corp. v. McClary, 879 F.3d 1114 (11th Cir. 2018)
United States v. Herring, 955 F.2d 703 (11th Cir. 1992)
Heller v. District of Columbia (Heller II), 670 F.3d 1244 (D.C. Cir. 2011) (Kavanaugh, J., dissenting)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson rightly emphasize that Bruen preserves a historically grounded “sensitive places” doctrine and that historians may assist courts with non-normative context under Rule 702, but that does not answer the core Bruen problem here: Hawaii’s categories, on this record, appear to extend the exception far beyond the concrete historical exemplars (legislative assemblies, polling places, courthouses) into broad swaths of ordinary public life. As Justice Kagan and Justice Barrett stress, defining “sensitivity” at a high level of generality risks converting a narrow carveout into a functional default prohibition, which Bruen specifically cautioned against, and expert testimony cannot supply the ultimate constitutional analogue or reintroduce interest balancing in historical dress. I am not persuaded that respondents have identified the kind of well-established, closely analogous tradition that would justify such an expansive map of presumptively forbidden locations, even while narrower, genuinely analogous sensitive-place limits remain permissible. The narrow, institutionally legitimate course is to reverse and remand for application of Bruen’s history-and-tradition test with the court—not experts—making the ultimate analogical judgment and with careful attention to overbreadth.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is that Hawaii may regulate carrying in historically recognized “sensitive places,” but under Bruen that category cannot be expanded to broad swaths of ordinary public life (parks, beaches, and other general congregation areas) absent a well-established, founding-era tradition of comparable location-based prohibitions. The Second Amendment’s text presumptively protects ordinary public carry, and the State must meet its burden with genuinely analogous historical regulations—not modern public-safety judgments repackaged as history. I agree with Justice Gorsuch and Justice Barrett that expert testimony may supply historical facts, but it cannot supply the ultimate constitutional rule or dilute Bruen’s burden allocation by substituting experts’ policy-inflected conclusions for judicial judgment. Nothing in the Respondents’ position identifies a sufficiently rooted tradition supporting a default prohibition or a near-comprehensive “sensitive places” map, so the regime as described cannot stand under Heller, McDonald, and Bruen.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right to emphasize that Bruen preserves a historically grounded "sensitive places" doctrine, and I accept (as Justice Jackson notes) that historians may provide non-normative context about what historical regulations actually did. But Bruen also cautions against defining sensitivity at a high level of generality such that ordinary public spaces become presumptively off-limits, and Hawaii’s broad coverage of parks, beaches, bars, and similar ubiquitous venues looks like the very sort of functional public-carry prohibition Bruen condemned absent a well-established analogue. Chief Justice Roberts’s point about Rule 702 is important: expert testimony may illuminate historical facts, but it cannot smuggle in interest balancing or supply the ultimate constitutional conclusion that these sweeping categories are “permitted.” On this record, the State’s justification remains too generalized and expert-driven to satisfy Bruen’s history-and-tradition burden, so reversal and remand is the proper course.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: I take seriously Justice Thomas’s and the Chief Justice’s strongest point: Bruen forbids expanding “sensitive places” by modern policy judgment and requires a genuine historical analogue rather than expert-driven conclusions. But that concern goes primarily to scope and methodology; it does not compel treating Hawaii’s location limits as per se unconstitutional where the State can tie particular categories to historically recognized restrictions in security-sensitive or densely congregated settings that Bruen itself preserved. I agree with Justice Kagan that the lower courts must not define sensitivity at too high a level of generality or let Rule 702 testimony substitute for the court’s analogical judgment, yet the appropriate remedy is a narrowing construction or remand to separate historically anchored locations from any overbroad “ordinary public life” sweep—not invalidation across the board. Because my approach focuses on real-world impacts and access to safety for vulnerable populations while still respecting Bruen’s burden allocation, I would uphold genuinely bounded sensitive-place prohibitions and require Hawaii to justify any broader exclusions with tighter historical proof.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point is that Bruen preserves a “sensitive places” doctrine and that densely congregated or security-sensitive venues can be regulated, but Bruen also warned against defining sensitivity at too high a level of generality—otherwise parks, beaches, and ordinary commercial districts become presumptively off-limits and the exception swallows the right. I agree with Chief Justice Roberts that the core defect here is methodological: whatever historians may contribute under Rule 702 (as Justice Jackson notes), the lower courts cannot let expert-driven narratives substitute for the court’s own analogical, historically tethered legal judgment or reintroduce interest balancing in historical dress. On this record, Hawaii has not identified a sufficiently close, well-established historical tradition to justify a sweeping map of ordinary public spaces as carry-free zones. The proper course is reversal and remand to apply Bruen with tighter attention to the specificity and fit of the asserted historical analogues while leaving room for genuinely narrow, historically grounded sensitive-place restrictions.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right that Bruen preserved a “sensitive places” carveout and that historians may supply contextual facts about historical enactments, but that does not answer the critical question of level of generality: parks, beaches, and ordinary commercial venues are not meaningfully analogous to the discrete, security-centric locations Bruen identified (courthouses, legislative assemblies, polling places). As the Chief Justice emphasizes, Rule 702 can help courts understand what historical laws did, but it cannot be used to outsource the ultimate constitutional analogical judgment or to reintroduce interest-balancing through expert labels of “sensitivity.” Justice Jackson’s point about allowing non-normative historical context is well-taken, yet on this record the State’s approach still risks converting the exception into the rule—functionally recreating the broad public-carry prohibitions Bruen rejected without the State carrying its burden with well-established historical analogues. I would therefore reverse and remand for a tighter, court-driven Bruen analysis that permits genuinely analogous sensitive-place restrictions but rejects sweeping, modern-policy-defined location bans.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right that Bruen preserves regulation in genuinely “sensitive places” and that historians can help explain what historical enactments did, but Bruen also warns against defining sensitivity at a high level of generality that would let modern policy judgments convert ordinary public life into default carry-free zones. As Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, Rule 702 may provide historical context, yet it cannot outsource the ultimate analogical constitutional judgment to experts or permit experts to reintroduce interest-balancing by opining on what the Second Amendment “allows.” Justice Jackson’s point that historians can offer non-normative assistance is sound, but it does not cure the overbreadth problem if Hawaii’s categories (parks, beaches, broad public venues) lack close historical analogues and thus functionally recreate the near-prohibitory regimes Bruen rejected. The institutionally proper disposition is to reverse and remand for a court-driven application of Bruen’s history-and-tradition test, allowing truly analogous sensitive-place restrictions while rejecting an untethered expansion that would swallow the right to bear arms.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right that Bruen preserves a historically grounded category of “sensitive places,” and that courts may uphold location-based limits where the State identifies a well-established analogue; but Bruen also warns against defining that category at a high level of generality untethered from concrete historical exemplars. As the Chief Justice notes, on this record Hawaii’s design appears to treat large portions of ordinary public life (parks, beaches, broad venues) as presumptively off-limits, which risks turning the exception into the rule in the manner Justice Kagan flags. I agree with Justice Jackson that historians can assist under Rule 702 with non-normative context, but I remain persuaded that expert testimony cannot supply the ultimate legal conclusion that such sweeping prohibitions reflect a relevantly similar historical tradition—courts must make that analogical judgment, and Hawaii has not carried its burden here. I would therefore reverse and remand for application of Bruen’s history-and-tradition test without importing interest balancing or allowing an overbroad “sensitive places” theory to do the work.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: I take Chief Justice Roberts’s point that Bruen forbids turning the “sensitive places” carveout into a functional default ban on ordinary public carry, and I agree with Justices Thomas and Kavanaugh that Rule 702 cannot outsource the ultimate constitutional judgment or reintroduce interest-balancing in expert form. But that methodological error does not require striking down Hawaii’s framework wholesale on this record; historians can still properly supply factual context about how historical location-based rules operated, with the court retaining the analogical/legal conclusion. Consistent with Heller and McDonald’s recognition of longstanding carveouts, I would sustain genuinely bounded, historically anchored location restrictions while remanding for a narrower application of Bruen’s burden allocation to any expansive, near-ubiquitous “default prohibition” features. The petitioners’ strongest point goes to overbreadth and the risk of exception-swallowing-the-right, but the appropriate remedy here is clarification and remand, not categorical invalidation.

John Roberts.reasoning: Bruen forecloses the lower courts’ resort to means-end scrutiny and public-safety balancing once the Second Amendment’s plain text covers public carry for self-defense, requiring instead that the State justify its restrictions by identifying a sufficiently analogous historical tradition of regulation. On this record, Hawaii’s approach—as described—leans on expert-driven legal conclusions and policy considerations in a way that risks substituting historians’ judgments for the court’s constitutional duty and diluting Heller and McDonald’s recognition of an individual right to keep and bear arms. While historical experts may assist with context, Bruen makes clear the ultimate analogical and constitutional judgment is for the courts, and a regime that effectively nullifies ordinary public carry cannot be sustained absent close historical analogues. A narrow disposition would reverse and remand with instructions to apply Bruen’s history-and-tradition test without interest balancing and without treating expert testimony as dispositive legal interpretation under Rule 702.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Second Amendment’s text protects the right of ordinary, law-abiding citizens to “bear Arms,” and Bruen holds that a State may restrict public carry only if it can justify its law by demonstrating a consistent historical tradition of firearm regulation, not by means-end or public-safety balancing. 597 U.S. 1 (2022). To the extent Hawaii’s regime functions as a broad default prohibition on public carry (or otherwise imposes sweeping location-based bans untethered to historically recognized “sensitive places”), it conflicts with Heller’s and McDonald’s recognition that the right belongs to the people and is not a second-class right subject to ad hoc interest balancing. 554 U.S. 570 (2008); 561 U.S. 742 (2010). Lower courts also err when they rely on expert testimony to supply legal conclusions about what the Second Amendment permits or to reintroduce policy balancing under the guise of historical interpretation; under Bruen, the constitutional question is one of law for the court, and the State bears the burden of producing genuinely analogous historical regulations rather than expert-driven reinterpretations that dilute the right.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Bruen held that the Second Amendment protects a right of ordinary, law-abiding citizens to carry handguns in public for self-defense and rejected the two-step approach that upheld restrictions through interest-balancing or public-safety tailoring. Under Bruen’s history-and-tradition test, Hawaii must identify well-established historical analogues for its modern carry restrictions, and broad limits that functionally deny or severely curtail public carry cannot be justified by generalized appeals to contemporary public safety. To the extent lower courts rely on expert testimony to supply legal conclusions about the meaning of the Second Amendment or to opine that Heller/McDonald/Bruen were historically wrong, that invades the court’s duty to decide questions of law and exceeds the proper scope of expert assistance under Fed. R. Evid. 702. Because the challenged regime appears to replicate the sort of ‘may-issue’ or near-prohibitory structure Bruen condemned, it likely violates the Second and Fourteenth Amendments.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Under Bruen, the State bears the burden to show that its public-carry limits are consistent with the Nation’s historical tradition of firearm regulation, and that inquiry permits courts to consider historically grounded restrictions on carrying in crowded or security-sensitive locations (including the “sensitive places” concept Bruen itself endorsed). Hawaii’s restrictions—aimed at locations like parks, beaches, bars, and similar public congregation spaces—fit within the longstanding tradition of regulating the manner and locations of public carry to protect public safety, especially where vulnerable populations and bystanders face heightened risk. The lower courts may use historians or other experts under Fed. R. Evid. 702 to supply context and meaning about historical enactments and practices, so long as experts do not offer ultimate legal conclusions about what the Second Amendment “requires,” which remains for judges under Heller, McDonald, and Bruen. Because Hawaii’s framework can be upheld through historical analogues rather than forbidden means-end balancing, I would vote to sustain it against the Second Amendment challenge.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Under N.Y. State Rifle & Pistol Ass’n v. Bruen, the State must justify a public-carry restriction by identifying a well-established historical analogue, and courts may not uphold the law by interest-balancing based on public-safety assessments. To the extent Hawaii’s scheme functions like the “may-issue” regimes Bruen rejected and is defended chiefly through expert-driven legal conclusions about what the Second Amendment permits, that approach both evades Bruen’s history-and-tradition inquiry and risks letting Rule 702-style expert testimony intrude on the court’s job to decide questions of law. Hawaii can regulate genuinely “sensitive places,” but Bruen cautioned against expanding that category by modern policy judgment rather than historically grounded limits (legislatures, polling places, courthouses), and the record described here suggests the lower courts leaned on balancing rather than close analogical fit. Because the State has not shown sufficiently analogous historical public-carry restrictions to support the breadth of the challenged limits, the restrictions are likely unconstitutional under Bruen (consistent with Heller and McDonald’s protection of an individual right).

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Second Amendment’s plain text covers carrying arms in public for self-defense, so Hawaii bears the burden under Bruen to justify its restrictions by demonstrating a well-established historical tradition of analogous regulation, not by invoking public-safety balancing or empirical policy judgments. Bruen expressly rejected means-end scrutiny and required courts to decide these questions as matters of law by consulting the relevant historical record, with expert testimony limited to assisting with historical facts rather than offering legal conclusions about what the Constitution permits (Fed. R. Evid. 702 cannot be used to outsource judicial interpretation). Reliance on a handful of outlier statutes—especially late, postbellum enactments—does not establish a tradition sufficient to overcome the presumption of protection recognized in Heller, McDonald, and Bruen. Because the lower court’s approach appears to dilute Bruen’s burden allocation and substitute expert-driven legal interpretation and balancing for the required history-and-tradition test, I would vote to reverse for the Petitioners.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Bruen holds that the Second Amendment protects a right for ordinary, law-abiding citizens to carry handguns publicly for self-defense and rejects interest-balancing or public-safety tailoring as the governing test; instead, the State must justify modern restrictions by identifying a relevant historical analogue within the Nation’s tradition of firearm regulation. To the extent Hawaii’s post-Bruen regime functionally recreates a “may-issue” denial or broadly criminalizes carry across ordinary public places by expanding “sensitive places” beyond what history supports, it conflicts with Bruen and Heller’s understanding of the right to “bear” arms. Lower courts may consider historians’ testimony to supply context about historical sources, but Rule 702 does not permit experts to opine on ultimate legal meaning—e.g., whether Heller/Bruen were “historically accurate” or how to apply the constitutional test—because those are legal conclusions reserved to the court. Applying judicial restraint and workability, enforcing Bruen’s history-and-tradition framework (rather than expert-driven legal reinterpretation or policy balancing) best preserves doctrinal stability and uniformity.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Under Bruen, once the regulated conduct (public carry by ordinary, law-abiding citizens for self-defense) falls within the Second Amendment’s plain text, the State must justify its restriction by identifying a relevant historical analogue, not by invoking public-safety balancing or tiered scrutiny. See New York State Rifle & Pistol Ass’n v. Bruen, 597 U.S. 1 (2022); District of Columbia v. Heller, 554 U.S. 570 (2008); McDonald v. City of Chicago, 561 U.S. 742 (2010). Hawaii’s defense—as framed here—leans heavily on expert-driven interpretations and policy considerations, but expert testimony cannot supply legal conclusions about “what the history means” in a way that displaces the court’s duty to determine the law, and Federal Rule of Evidence 702 does not authorize experts to opine on ultimate legal questions. Because the State has not shown that the challenged public-carry restrictions align with a well-established founding-era tradition at an appropriately specific level of generality, the restrictions likely violate the Second Amendment.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Under Bruen, Hawaii bears the burden to justify its public-carry restrictions by demonstrating consistency with the Nation’s historical tradition of firearm regulation, including limits on armed carriage in historically recognized “sensitive places,” such as legislative assemblies, polling places, and courthouses. Bruen also makes clear that courts may not uphold restrictions through freestanding public-safety or empirical interest-balancing, but it does not preclude the use of historians or other experts to provide contextual, non-normative assistance about how historical laws operated; Rule 702 permits such testimony so long as it does not supply legal conclusions that usurp the court’s role. On this record, I would not invalidate Hawaii’s regime wholesale merely because the lower courts considered expert-driven historical context, and I would allow regulations that are properly limited to historically analogous sensitive places and comparable longstanding public-carry controls. Consistent with Heller and McDonald, the Second Amendment protects an individual right, but it also tolerates historically grounded regulation, and Hawaii’s narrower, historically anchored restrictions can coexist with that right.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Hawaii’s restrictions on carrying firearms (and the Ninth Circuit’s method of evaluating them) violate the Second and Fourteenth Amendments under the Supreme Court’s text-and-history test, and relatedly whether courts may rely on expert testimony that amounts to legal conclusions about founding-era law.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. amend. II (as incorporated against the States through U.S. Const. amend. XIV); applied through the analytical framework announced in New York State Rifle & Pistol Ass’n, Inc. v. Bruen.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners argue that the Second Amendment’s plain text protects ordinary citizens’ right to carry firearms for self-defense and that Hawaii’s carry regime improperly burdens or effectively nullifies that right. Under Bruen, once the conduct is covered by the text, Hawaii must prove its law is consistent with the Nation’s historical tradition of firearm regulation; generalized public-safety balancing, social-science evidence, or modern policy preferences cannot justify suppressing the core right (as emphasized in Heller and McDonald). Petitioners (and amici) also contend that lower courts may not dilute Supreme Court holdings by recasting them, and that ‘historical’ expert testimony that tells courts how to interpret founding-era statutes/law is inadmissible because it crosses from historical fact into legal interpretation—a question reserved to judges rather than experts under Rule 702 principles.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondent (Hawaii) defends its carry restrictions as constitutionally permissible under Bruen by asserting that historical analogues support regulating the public carry of firearms, especially in the interest of public safety. Hawaii also relies on historical scholarship and expert presentations to frame how founding-era and Reconstruction-era laws should be understood and analogized to modern regulations. In addition, Hawaii resists the view that its law ‘obliterates’ the right, arguing instead that the Second Amendment allows meaningful regulation and that its regime fits within a historically grounded tradition of limiting armed carry in sensitive contexts or for public safety reasons.
key_precedents: District of Columbia v. Heller, 554 U.S. 570 (2008)
McDonald v. City of Chicago, 561 U.S. 742 (2010)
New York State Rifle & Pistol Ass’n, Inc. v. Bruen, 597 U.S. 1 (2022)
Commodores Entertainment Corp. v. McClary, 879 F.3d 1114 (11th Cir. 2018)
United States v. Herring, 955 F.2d 703 (11th Cir. 1992)
Heller v. District of Columbia (Heller II), 670 F.3d 1244 (D.C. Cir. 2011) (Kavanaugh, J., dissenting) (as quoted)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s and Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point—that we should not treat Hawaii’s regime as a de facto ban without a clearer operational record, and that the proper remedy is methodological correction rather than outright invalidation—counsels in favor of restraint, but it does not justify affirmance on the Ninth Circuit’s approach. Bruen squarely assigns the burden to the State to produce a well-established historical analogue with a comparable burden and justification, and as Justice Thomas emphasizes, courts cannot dilute that burden by allowing “sensitive places” to expand elastically or by effectively outsourcing the analogical legal judgment to experts. Justice Jackson is right that historians can supply context, but that reinforces (rather than undermines) a narrow disposition: vacate and remand with instructions to apply Bruen faithfully, evaluate the law’s real-world burden, and treat expert testimony as factual/contextual support—not as dispositive legal conclusions. This course addresses Respondents’ record-based concern while preserving the institutional legitimacy of enforcing Bruen’s methodology without deciding more than necessary today.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s and Justice Kagan’s best point—that Heller/McDonald and Bruen tolerate historically grounded limits in genuinely sensitive places and that we should hesitate absent a clearer operational record—does not answer Bruen’s threshold demand that the State identify a well-established historical analogue with a comparable burden and justification. The “meaningful avenue for carry” framing risks reintroducing a reasonableness or interest-balancing inquiry untethered from the Second Amendment’s original public meaning; it cannot substitute for the historical-tradition showing Bruen makes dispositive. I agree with Chief Justice Roberts that experts may supply historical facts and context, but the Ninth Circuit cannot defer to expert legal conclusions about what sources mean or whether they are analogous, because that is the court’s constitutional duty. Given the breadth and practical effect described, and the absence of a founding- or Reconstruction-era tradition supporting such a sweeping place-based exclusion, I would at least vacate and remand for application of Bruen without diluting the State’s burden through an elastic “sensitive places” category.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s and Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point—that Heller/McDonald and Bruen allow historically grounded restrictions in truly sensitive places and that a regime may stand if it leaves a “meaningful avenue” for carry—does not answer Bruen’s core demand that the State identify a well-established analogue comparable in both burden and justification. Even accepting Justice Jackson’s concern about an underdeveloped operational record, the Ninth Circuit’s methodology cannot be sustained if it effectively permits the State to designate broad swaths of ordinary public life as “sensitive” without a close historical match, because that risks the very functional nullification Bruen forbids. I agree with Chief Justice Roberts that historians may supply context, but the constitutional judgment of analogy is for judges; expert testimony cannot substitute for that legal conclusion. On this record, Respondent still has not identified founding- or Reconstruction-era place-based restrictions of comparable breadth and practical effect, so reversal or, at minimum, vacatur and remand with strict instructions to apply Bruen faithfully remains the proper course.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito make the strongest petitioner point: Bruen forbids using an elastic “sensitive places” label to accomplish a de facto public-carry ban, and the State bears the historical burden. I agree with Chief Justice Roberts’s narrower institutional concern that the Ninth Circuit must not treat expert testimony as a substitute for the court’s own analogical judgment under Bruen; that is a serious methodological flaw that can warrant vacatur and remand. But that critique does not, by itself, establish that Hawaii’s scheme is operationally equivalent to the may-issue denial regime Bruen struck down, and without a clearer showing that ordinary, law-abiding citizens are left with no meaningful avenue to carry, I am not prepared to invalidate the law wholesale. Under my pragmatic approach, the proper course is to enforce Bruen’s burden and judicial role while resisting a merits reversal premised on assumptions about real-world effects not firmly found in this record.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito are right to insist Bruen forbids States from converting most public space into “sensitive places” as a workaround, and I share Chief Justice Roberts’s concern that the Ninth Circuit may have let expert “analogue” testimony displace the court’s own constitutional judgment. But that principle does not itself resolve this case on the present record, because the key question is whether Hawaii’s designations and exceptions, in operation, are comparably burdensome to historically recognized place-based limits or instead function as a near-ban; I do not think we can assume the latter without a tighter, court-driven analogical analysis. Roberts’s proposed vacatur-and-remand path best enforces Bruen’s allocation of burdens and the judiciary’s duty to decide analogy while avoiding an overbroad merits holding that could wrongly constitutionalize maximal carry in all ordinary places. Under my pragmatic textualist approach, the coherent remedy is to require the lower court to apply Bruen correctly—demanding genuine historical comparability in both burden and justification—rather than to invalidate outright absent clearer findings on practical availability of lawful carry.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s strongest point—that Heller and McDonald allow historically grounded, place-based limits and that the right is not violated unless the scheme becomes a de facto ban—does not undermine my view because Bruen makes the State’s burden dispositive: it must identify a genuinely analogous historical tradition with a comparable burden and justification, not rely on an expandable “sensitive places” label or generalized safety rationales. Justice Sotomayor’s and Justice Jackson’s emphasis on an underdeveloped “operational record” may counsel a remand rather than a merits invalidation, but it does not supply the missing analogue, and the constitutional inquiry cannot be replaced by a free-floating “meaningful avenue for carry” standard. I agree with Chief Justice Roberts that historians may inform historical facts and context, yet courts cannot outsource the legal judgment of analogy to expert testimony without effectively reintroducing deference by another name. On the arguments presented, respondent has not carried Bruen’s historical-analogue burden for a restriction of this breadth and practical effect, so I remain with petitioner (at minimum for vacatur and remand with instructions to apply Bruen faithfully).

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor make the respondent’s best point: Bruen preserves historically grounded regulation of genuinely “sensitive places,” and we should be cautious about deciding on an undeveloped operational record. But that caution cuts toward Chief Justice Roberts’s narrower remedy—vacatur and remand—not affirmance, because Bruen squarely places the burden on the State to produce a distinctly similar historical analogue in both burden and justification, and the Ninth Circuit cannot dilute that burden by reframing the test as whether some “meaningful avenue” remains. I also agree with Justice Thomas (and the Chief) that experts may supply context, but courts cannot defer to expert legal conclusions about what counts as an “analogue,” or else history becomes a proxy for interest-balancing that Bruen forbids. On the arguments presented, respondent has not identified a well-established founding- or Reconstruction-era tradition supporting a regime that—if it operates as described—effectively denies ordinary, law-abiding citizens practical public carry across large swaths of everyday life, so I remain for petitioner at least for vacatur/remand under a faithful Bruen analysis.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor offer the strongest respondent point: Heller and McDonald recognize the right is not unlimited and permit historically grounded limits in genuinely “sensitive places,” potentially consistent with a regime that leaves some meaningful avenue for carry. But under Bruen, that “meaningful avenue” idea cannot substitute for the State’s affirmative burden to produce a well-established historical analogue comparable in both burden and justification; otherwise it becomes a form of interest-balancing and invites States to deem ordinary public spaces “sensitive” in a way that swallows the rule. Chief Justice Roberts’s emphasis on not outsourcing the constitutional judgment to experts reinforces—rather than undermines—vacatur and remand here, because the lower court must itself perform the analogical analysis instead of treating expert conclusions as dispositive. Given the absence, on this record as framed, of a sufficiently close founding- or Reconstruction-era tradition supporting a broad, operationally severe place-based carry prohibition, I remain with petitioner at least for vacatur and remand under a faithful Bruen methodology.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Roberts’s proposed vacatur-and-remand framework persuades me that my operational-record concerns can be addressed without effectively insulating the Ninth Circuit’s analysis from Bruen’s burden shift. I continue to think Justice Sotomayor is right that we should not assume, without careful findings, that Hawaii’s scheme is a de facto ban; but Justice Thomas and Justice Alito correctly press that Bruen does not tolerate an elastic “sensitive places” category that risks swallowing the right, and the lower court’s methodology appears to have let expert testimony do work that belongs to judges. Under my pragmatic lens, procedural fairness and institutional competence cut toward requiring a court-driven analogical analysis (with experts limited to context/facts), and a remand is the appropriate remedy to ensure that discipline while assessing real-world burdens. Accordingly, I would join the petitioner at least for vacatur and remand with clear instructions, rather than affirming on this record.

John Roberts.reasoning: Under Bruen, once the Second Amendment’s plain text covers ordinary, law-abiding citizens carrying handguns in public for self-defense, the State bears the burden to justify its restrictions by showing consistency with the Nation’s historical tradition of firearm regulation, not by invoking modern public-safety balancing or means-end scrutiny. Where the Ninth Circuit’s approach effectively permits broad “sensitive place” expansions or other carry limits that functionally negate the public-carry right recognized in Bruen, the decision risks conflicting with Heller and McDonald and undermining uniformity in constitutional standards. On the evidentiary issue, expert testimony may assist with historical facts, but courts must not outsource legal interpretation of founding-era law to experts; determining the meaning and relevance of historical sources under Bruen is a judicial function. A narrow disposition would vacate and remand for application of Bruen’s text-and-history methodology without reliance on expert opinions that amount to legal conclusions.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Second Amendment’s text protects the right to “bear” arms, and Bruen holds that when the plain text covers public carry by law-abiding citizens, the State must justify restrictions by demonstrating a well-established historical tradition of analogous regulation—not by means-end scrutiny or generalized public-safety balancing. Hawaii’s regime, to the extent it effectively conditions ordinary public carry on broad prohibitions or discretionary judgments, conflicts with Bruen’s command and cannot be sustained absent a close historical analogue from the founding or Reconstruction era consistent with the original public meaning as recognized in Heller and incorporated against the States in McDonald. The Ninth Circuit’s approach is improper if it dilutes this Court’s text-and-history test or permits “expert” testimony to supply legal conclusions about what founding-era law means, a question for judges rather than witnesses. Because Hawaii has not carried its burden under Bruen to show its carry restrictions fit within the Nation’s historical tradition, the Second and Fourteenth Amendments are violated.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Under Bruen, once the Second Amendment’s plain text covers ordinary citizens’ public carry for self-defense, the State must justify its restrictions by showing they are consistent with the Nation’s historical tradition of firearm regulation, not by interest-balancing or modern policy judgments. Hawaii’s regime—if it functions to broadly criminalize or effectively nullify public carry for law-abiding citizens—conflicts with Heller’s insistence that the core right cannot be reduced to a “second-class” guarantee and with McDonald’s incorporation of that right against the States through the Fourteenth Amendment. The Ninth Circuit’s approach is unconstitutional to the extent it dilutes Bruen’s text-and-history test by relying on expert testimony that supplies legal conclusions about founding-era law, because interpreting historical sources as law is the judge’s task, not an expert’s under Rule 702 principles. Practical consequences also counsel against allowing States to evade Bruen by re-labeling broad carry prohibitions as “regulation,” thereby undermining uniform constitutional protections.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Under Bruen, the State bears the burden to justify modern carry restrictions by demonstrating a relevant historical tradition of regulating public carry, especially in crowded or sensitive places, and Hawaii may satisfy that burden with properly framed historical analogues rather than modern interest-balancing. Heller and McDonald recognize an individual right but also make clear the right is not unlimited and is compatible with longstanding regulations; that caution counsels against treating the Second Amendment as disabling reasonable public-carry regulation that protects vulnerable communities from gun violence. The Ninth Circuit may consider expert historical testimony to illuminate historical facts and context, but courts must independently decide the legal meaning of founding-era sources and should not defer to experts’ legal conclusions, consistent with the judge’s role in constitutional interpretation. On this record, I would uphold Hawaii’s regime insofar as it leaves a meaningful avenue for lawful carry while permitting targeted restrictions grounded in history and tradition.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Under Bruen, Hawaii bears the burden to show its public-carry restrictions are consistent with the Nation’s historical tradition of firearm regulation, and the analysis turns on whether the State’s regime is a relevantly similar analogue to historically accepted limits on armed carry in public, including in sensitive places or for public-safety reasons. On this record, I would not treat Bruen or Heller as foreclosing all meaningful public-carry regulation; both recognize an individual right but also preserve room for historically grounded regulations, and McDonald incorporates that right against the States without disabling them from regulating within that tradition. I would, however, clarify that while historians may testify to historical facts and context, courts may not outsource the legal judgment of what history means for constitutionality to experts—consistent with Bruen’s directive that judges apply the text-and-history test rather than means-end scrutiny or policy balancing. Because Hawaii’s position plausibly fits within a historically anchored tradition and the Ninth Circuit’s errors (if any) can be corrected without invalidating the law on this record, I would affirm for the Respondent.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Under Bruen, once the Second Amendment’s plain text covers an individual’s proposed conduct—carrying a handgun in public for self-defense—the State bears the burden to justify its restriction by showing it is consistent with the Nation’s historical tradition of firearm regulation, not by invoking modern public-safety balancing or social-science evidence. Hawaii’s regime, to the extent it operates like a discretionary or effectively prohibitory carry system for ordinary, law-abiding citizens, conflicts with Bruen’s holding that such citizens possess a right to bear arms in public, and with Heller and McDonald’s rejection of interest-balancing tests that dilute the Amendment’s core protection. The Ninth Circuit’s reliance on expert testimony that supplies legal conclusions about what founding-era law “means” risks substituting litigant-driven “history-and-tradition” gloss for judicial interpretation; courts may consider historical facts and sources, but the interpretation of law remains a judicial function, and any ambiguity about criminal prohibitions should be resolved consistent with the rule of lenity. Applying Bruen’s text-and-history framework, Hawaii must point to genuinely analogous historical regulations (comparable in burden and justification), and absent that showing, the restrictions violate the Second and Fourteenth Amendments.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Under Bruen, once the Second Amendment’s text covers the conduct—ordinary, law-abiding citizens carrying handguns in public for self-defense—the State bears the burden to justify its restrictions by identifying a distinctly similar historical analogue from the founding or Reconstruction era, not by invoking modern public-safety balancing or means-end scrutiny. Hawaii’s regime, to the extent it functionally denies or substantially burdens public carry for typical citizens, conflicts with Heller and McDonald’s recognition of an individual right to possess and carry arms for self-defense and Bruen’s rejection of interest-balancing as a substitute for history and tradition. The Ninth Circuit’s approach cannot dilute this Court’s framework by reintroducing policy-based analysis under another label, and courts must independently interpret historical legal materials rather than accept expert testimony that amounts to legal conclusions about what founding-era law “means.” The proper disposition is to reverse and require application of Bruen’s text-and-history test consistent with this Court’s precedents.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Under Bruen, once the Second Amendment’s plain text covers carrying arms in public for self-defense, the State bears the burden to justify its restriction by demonstrating consistency with the Nation’s historical tradition of firearm regulation, not by interest balancing or generalized public-safety rationales. Bruen held that may-issue regimes that condition public carry on discretionary need findings violate the Second and Fourteenth Amendments, and Heller and McDonald likewise reject means-end scrutiny that dilutes the core right. To the extent Hawaii’s regime (as applied or in practical operation) functions like a discretionary or near-prohibitory carry system without close historical analogues, it fails Bruen’s text-and-history test. Courts may consider historical evidence, but expert testimony cannot supply legal conclusions about what founding-era law “means,” because interpreting law is for judges and Bruen requires judicial application of the historical-analogy methodology rather than deference to expert legal interpretation.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Under Bruen, Hawaii must justify its public-carry restrictions by demonstrating a relevant historical tradition of regulating the manner of armed carry, particularly in sensitive places and for public-safety-related constraints, rather than by means-end scrutiny or freestanding interest balancing. On this record, I would not treat the Ninth Circuit’s consideration of historical scholarship and expert context as categorically improper; courts may rely on experts for historical facts and context so long as judges themselves decide the legal meaning of the Second and Fourteenth Amendments and the controlling analogical inquiry demanded by Bruen and Heller. Given the State’s latitude to enact regulations that do not amount to a de facto ban on ordinary, law-abiding citizens’ ability to carry for self-defense (Bruen), and mindful of practical consequences and administrability, I would uphold Hawaii’s regime absent a clearer showing that it functionally nullifies the right recognized in Bruen. Accordingly, I would affirm for Respondent while emphasizing that lower courts must police the boundary between admissible historical evidence and impermissible expert legal conclusions under evidentiary principles akin to Rule 702.
